questions.explanation_es: Típicamente hay un breve período durante el cual el tráfico destinado a la MAC del gateway virtual puede perderse o retrasarse, ya que el nuevo router Active necesita empezar a responder por esa MAC/IP virtual, y cualquier entrada de caché ARP en tránsito en los hosts finales apuntando a la asociación de MAC física anterior podría necesitar un momento para refrescarse, aunque HSRP está diseñado para hacer esta transición lo más rápida razonablemente posible.

questions.name: HSRP/VRRP
questions.question: Why is it important that the FHRP hello/hold (or advertisement) timers be configured consistently across all routers participating in the same group?

options.A: Mismatched timers between group members could cause one router to declare the other dead prematurely (based on its own shorter hold timer) even though the peer is actually still sending hellos at its own longer configured interval, potentially causing unnecessary or inconsistent failover behavior between the members of that same group
options.B: FHRP timers have no relationship whatsoever to failover behavior, and mismatched timers between group members produce exactly identical behavior to matched timers in every possible scenario
options.C: Timer configuration only matters for VRRP and has absolutely no relevance whatsoever to HSRP, which is described as being fundamentally incapable of using any configurable hello or hold timer at all
options.D: A mismatched timer configuration between group members always and immediately prevents the FHRP group from forming at all, refusing to elect any Active/Master router whatsoever until the mismatch is corrected

questions.explanation_es: Temporizadores desajustados entre miembros del grupo podrían causar que un router declare al otro muerto prematuramente (basándose en su propio hold timer más corto) aunque el peer en realidad siga enviando hellos a su propio intervalo configurado más largo, potencialmente causando comportamiento de failover innecesario o inconsistente entre los miembros de ese mismo grupo.

questions.name: Multicast
questions.question: What command is commonly used to view the current multicast routing table (mroute table) on a Cisco router?

options.A: 'show ip mroute', which displays active multicast (S,G) and (*,G) entries, including incoming and outgoing interface information for each multicast group/source pair
options.B: 'show ip route', which only displays the unicast routing table and has no relationship whatsoever to multicast-specific routing entries
options.C: The multicast routing table can never be viewed through any Cisco IOS command output, and can only be inferred indirectly by capturing packets on every interface
options.D: 'show vlan brief' displays the multicast routing table directly alongside VLAN-to-port assignments, with no separate multicast-specific command needed

questions.explanation_es: 'show ip mroute' muestra las entradas multicast (S,G) y (*,G) activas, incluyendo información de interfaz entrante y saliente para cada par grupo/fuente multicast.

questions.name: Multicast
questions.question: What is the difference between a '(*,G)' and an '(S,G)' entry in a multicast routing table?

options.A: A (*,G) entry represents the shared tree for a given group G (rooted at the RP, matching traffic from any source), while an (S,G) entry represents the source-specific tree for a particular source S sending to group G, which is more specific and typically results from either an SPT-switchover or SSM's direct source-specific join
options.B: (*,G) and (S,G) entries represent exactly the same information with no meaningful distinction between them, differing only in notation style with no actual difference in what tree or traffic each one represents
options.C: A (*,G) entry can only ever exist in PIM Dense Mode, and is technically unsupported in PIM Sparse Mode, which is described as using only (S,G) entries
options.D: An (S,G) entry represents traffic from every possible source combined, while a (*,G) entry represents traffic from exactly one single specific source, the reverse of how the two entry types are actually defined

questions.explanation_es: Una entrada (*,G) representa el árbol compartido para un grupo G dado (enraizado en el RP, coincidiendo con tráfico de cualquier fuente), mientras que una entrada (S,G) representa el árbol específico de fuente para una fuente S en particular enviando al grupo G, lo cual es más específico y típicamente resulta de un SPT-switchover o de un join directo específico de fuente de SSM.

questions.name: Multicast
questions.question: Why might an organization use multicast for delivering routine software updates or OS images simultaneously to a large number of devices on the same network segment?

options.A: Multicast lets a single stream of update data reach many recipient devices simultaneously without the source needing to send a completely separate unicast copy to each individual device, which can dramatically reduce the total bandwidth consumed and total time needed compared to sequentially or simultaneously unicasting the same large file to every device one connection at a time
options.B: Multicast delivery of software updates provides no bandwidth or time efficiency benefit whatsoever compared to sending a fully separate unicast copy of the same update to every single individual recipient device
options.C: Multicast can only ever deliver data to a maximum of exactly one single recipient device at a time, making it functionally identical to unicast rather than offering any one-to-many efficiency benefit
options.D: Using multicast for this purpose always and completely prevents any device from actually receiving the update data correctly, making it fundamentally unsuitable for any file-delivery use case like software updates

questions.explanation_es: El multicast le permite a un único stream de datos de actualización llegar a muchos dispositivos receptores simultáneamente sin que la fuente necesite enviar una copia unicast completamente separada a cada dispositivo individual, lo cual puede reducir drásticamente el ancho de banda total consumido y el tiempo total necesario comparado con hacer unicast secuencial o simultáneo del mismo archivo grande a cada dispositivo una conexión a la vez.

questions.name: Multicast
questions.question: What potential security consideration arises from the fact that, by default, any host on a network segment can typically send an IGMP join to receive traffic for any multicast group it wants?

options.A: Without additional controls (such as an access-list restricting which groups a host is permitted to join, or IGMP snooping with appropriate filtering), an unauthorized or unintended host could potentially join and receive multicast traffic that wasn't meant for it, so some deployments apply filtering to restrict which multicast groups specific hosts/ports are permitted to join
options.B: IGMP joins have no security implications whatsoever, since multicast traffic is always automatically restricted at the network layer to only the specific host(s) that legitimately originated the underlying application session
options.C: Multicast group membership can only ever be controlled by physically disconnecting a host's cable, since IGMP itself provides absolutely no mechanism of any kind for restricting or filtering which groups a given host may join
options.D: This consideration only applies to source-specific multicast (SSM) and has no relevance whatsoever to any-source multicast using PIM-SM with a shared tree

questions.explanation_es: Sin controles adicionales (como una access-list restringiendo a qué grupos tiene permitido unirse un host, o IGMP snooping con filtrado apropiado), un host no autorizado o no pretendido podría potencialmente unirse y recibir tráfico multicast que no estaba pensado para él, así que algunos despliegues aplican filtrado para restringir a qué grupos multicast tienen permitido unirse hosts/puertos específicos.

questions.name: Multicast
questions.question: Why is PIM itself (the protocol routers use to build multicast distribution trees) generally considered a control-plane protocol distinct from the actual multicast data traffic it helps route?

options.A: PIM messages (joins, prunes, hellos, assert messages) are exchanged between routers to build and maintain the multicast distribution tree structure and determine which interfaces should forward a given group's traffic, while the actual multicast data packets themselves are a separate thing being forwarded according to the state PIM establishes — similar in spirit to how a unicast routing protocol like OSPF builds the routing table used to forward unrelated unicast data traffic
options.B: PIM and multicast data traffic are exactly the same thing with no meaningful distinction between the control-plane signaling protocol and the actual application data being distributed via multicast
options.C: PIM messages themselves carry the actual multicast application data payload directly within them, rather than being a separate control-plane signaling mechanism used to build forwarding state for that data
options.D: There is no relationship whatsoever between PIM and how multicast data traffic is actually forwarded through the network; PIM exclusively handles an entirely unrelated function like device inventory management

questions.explanation_es: Los mensajes de PIM (joins, prunes, hellos, mensajes assert) se intercambian entre routers para construir y mantener la estructura del árbol de distribución multicast y determinar qué interfaces deberían reenviar el tráfico de un grupo dado, mientras que los propios paquetes de datos multicast son algo separado que se reenvía según el estado que PIM establece — de forma conceptualmente similar a cómo un protocolo de enrutamiento unicast como OSPF construye la tabla de enrutamiento usada para reenviar tráfico de datos unicast no relacionado.

questions.name: Multicast
questions.question: What is a practical reason an organization deploying IP video/broadcast services over multicast would need to carefully plan IGMP snooping configuration on every Layer 2 switch in the path between source and receivers?

options.A: Without properly functioning IGMP snooping on every intermediate switch, multicast traffic might either be unnecessarily flooded to every port in the VLAN (wasting bandwidth on links with no actual interested receiver) or, if misconfigured, might fail to reach a port that does have a legitimate receiver, so consistent, correctly functioning snooping configuration across the entire Layer 2 path is important for both efficiency and correct delivery
options.B: IGMP snooping configuration only matters on the very first switch closest to the multicast source, and has absolutely no relevance whatsoever to any switch further downstream toward the actual receivers
options.C: IGMP snooping has no relationship whatsoever to how efficiently or correctly multicast traffic is delivered across a Layer 2 switched path, and exists purely as an optional cosmetic feature with zero practical forwarding impact
options.D: Every Layer 2 switch is assumed to always forward multicast traffic with perfect efficiency and correctness by default, with absolutely no IGMP snooping configuration of any kind ever actually required for correct multicast delivery

questions.explanation_es: Sin IGMP snooping funcionando correctamente en cada switch intermedio, el tráfico multicast podría inundarse innecesariamente hacia cada puerto de la VLAN (desperdiciando ancho de banda en enlaces sin ningún receptor interesado real) o, si está mal configurado, podría no llegar a un puerto que sí tiene un receptor legítimo, así que una configuración de snooping consistente y correctamente funcional en todo el camino de Capa 2 es importante tanto para la eficiencia como para la entrega correcta.
